questions.question: A component receives price and quantity as props, keeps total in useState, and syncs it with a useEffect calling setTotal(price * quantity). The React docs flag this as their most common code smell — why?
choices: The Effect is missing a cleanup function to cancel the pending setTotal before the next run
Calling a state setter inside an Effect violates the Rules of Hooks, which forbid hooks below the top level
Derived values should be computed during render; mirroring one into state adds an extra render pass and risks total drifting out of sync
total should live in a useRef instead, since refs persist across renders without triggering re-renders
questions.explanation: State that mirrors a computable value creates two sources of truth: the component first renders with the stale total, then the Effect fires and forces a second render — and any code path that updates one side but not the other makes them drift. Anything derivable from props or state should be a plain expression in render (const total = price * quantity); Effects are reserved for synchronizing with external systems, and nothing external is involved here. Cleanup solves stale async results, not derivation; calling a setter in an Effect is legal under the Rules of Hooks; and a ref would hide the value from rendering entirely.

questions.question: Two users vote at the same instant; both requests run choice.votes += 1 then choice.save(), and one vote is lost. Which change removes the race, and why?
choices: Wrap the read and the save in transaction.atomic() so the two requests serialize
Assign choice.votes = F('votes') + 1 before save(), so the increment happens inside the UPDATE statement, in the database
Call save(update_fields=['votes']) so only the votes column is written back
Move the increment into a post_save signal so it runs exactly once per saved instance
questions.explanation: The bug is a read-modify-write race: both requests read votes=N in Python and both write back N+1. F() pushes the arithmetic into SQL — UPDATE ... SET votes = votes + 1 — so the database applies each increment atomically no matter how the requests interleave. transaction.atomic gives all-or-nothing commit, not isolation: both transactions can still read the same starting value. update_fields only narrows which columns are written, still carrying the stale Python-side value, and a signal merely relocates the same racy code.

questions.question: A local Docker stack has no AWS access. For a file-uploads feature the team weighs (a) a dev-only local-filesystem storage branch versus (b) running MinIO as a container. What is the main architectural argument for MinIO?
choices: MinIO's web console gives developers a UI to inspect uploaded files, which a bare filesystem cannot offer
MinIO persists objects across container restarts, while a local filesystem loses them
The S3 API handles large uploads faster than local filesystem I/O
The same boto3/S3 code path runs unchanged in every environment — only the endpoint differs — so no untested dev-only branch can drift from production
questions.explanation: A filesystem fallback is a code path that never executes in production, which is exactly how storage bugs hide until deploy: the branch quietly drifts because nothing exercises it against real behavior. MinIO serves the actual S3 API, so swapping it for AWS is a change of address, not of code — one path, exercised locally exactly as in prod. The console is a convenience, not the argument; a filesystem persists fine (MinIO also needs a mounted volume); and raw local I/O is generally faster than any HTTP API, so performance argues the other way.

questions.question: Bagging (Random Forests) trains deep trees in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them; boosting trains small trees sequentially, each fit to the ensemble's remaining errors. Which failure mode does each architecture attack?
choices: Bagging reduces variance by cancelling uncorrelated errors across trees; boosting reduces bias by successively removing systematic error
Bagging reduces bias by averaging away systematic error; boosting reduces variance by keeping each tree small
Both reduce variance — boosting is simply a faster route to the same ensemble average
Bagging eliminates overfitting entirely; boosting trades bias for variance through the learning rate
questions.explanation: Averaging many independently-trained, unstable trees cancels noise that points in different directions — variance drops — but an error every tree shares survives the average (the ρσ² floor in Var(mean) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/k), so bias stays put. Boosting flips the architecture: each new tree studies what the running sum still gets wrong, shaving off systematic error round after round — which is also why gradient boosting can overfit and needs shrinkage and early stopping where a Random Forest mostly saturates. The two are complementary answers to the single-tree bias/variance trade-off, not interchangeable speedups.

questions.question: A service function decorated with @transaction.atomic saves an uploaded file to object storage, then creates the related DB rows; row creation raises. What must the except block do, and why?
choices: Nothing — atomic() rolls back the whole operation, including the stored file
Re-raise inside a nested atomic() block so a savepoint also covers the file write
Delete the stored blob explicitly before re-raising: storage writes are never enrolled in the DB transaction, so rollback alone leaves an orphaned file
Call save(update_fields=[]) on the document so no partially-written rows persist
questions.explanation: transaction.atomic rolls back rows, not side effects: a blob written to disk or object storage sits outside the database transaction, so on exception the rows vanish but the file survives as an orphan. The seam must track what it wrote and clean up itself — doc.file.delete(save=False), then re-raise so the DB rollback still happens. Nested atomic() blocks only add savepoints over DB state, and update_fields shapes a future write rather than undoing anything. This is also why validating everything before the first write is so valuable: a rejection then needs no cleanup at all.

questions.question: You train LightGBM with objective='quantile', alpha=0.95 for an SLA upper bound, then compare it against the default L2 model using RMSE — and the quantile model looks strictly worse. What is the methodological error?
choices: alpha=0.95 is too extreme for RMSE; re-comparing both models at alpha=0.5 would make the metric valid
RMSE is minimised by predicting the conditional mean, so it structurally favours the L2 model; a quantile model must be judged with pinball loss at its own alpha
The quantile model should have been trained with metric='rmse' so that training and evaluation objectives match
Nothing — the comparison is valid and shows the L2 model produces the better upper bound
questions.explanation: Choosing a loss chooses the statistic you estimate: squared error is minimised by the mean, pinball loss at alpha by that quantile. A model deliberately pushed up to the 95th percentile will always score worse on RMSE — that says nothing about how well it estimates the quantile, which is the thing the SLA needs. The right yardstick is pinball loss at the model's own alpha (metric='quantile' or mean_pinball_loss). Re-comparing at alpha=0.5 doesn't help — that targets the median, still not the mean — and setting an RMSE metric on a quantile objective just misreports training progress instead of fixing the mismatch.

questions.question: "As a QA engineer, I can have the test database restart automatically each night, so that I can test faster." Which trap is this, and what is the tell?
choices: Fake Story — the need sits inside the team's own Zone of Control; it is an internal task dressed in story costume
Misleading Story — the goal prescribes a technical solution while hiding the real underlying problem
Dependency-Locked — the deliverable depends on infrastructure outside the team's control
Micro-Story — it is sliced so thin it carries no standalone business risk
questions.explanation: A healthy story's need lives in the Sphere of Influence — user behaviour, business outcomes the team can affect but not control — while its deliverable sits in the Zone of Control. Here both the beneficiary and the need are inside the team: nothing about a user or the business is at stake, so there is no risk the story format exists to manage — the team is writing itself tickets. The honest fix is to track it as a Task, not to reject the work. A Misleading Story differs in that a genuine user need exists but is hidden behind a prescribed mechanism; here there is no external need at all.

questions.question: In Context-Anchored Specifications, every dictionary-sense use of a term in Stories and AC must be backticked. What design goal turns this rule from decoration into infrastructure?
choices: Backticks render terms in monospace, making specifications easier for stakeholders to scan
It lets a linter verify that code classes and endpoints are named after Dictionary terms
It prevents authors from using undefined terms, since a backtick requires an existing Dictionary entry
When a definition changes, grepping the backticked term mechanically yields exactly the artifacts that need re-review — the Dictionary becomes a navigable index of the spec
questions.explanation: Highlighting (Rule 1) exists to serve propagation (Rule 9): when a term's meaning shifts mid-iteration, the re-review set is precisely the Stories and AC whose text contains the backticked term — a mechanical grep, not a memory exercise. Without that propagation contract, the highlighting overhead buys nothing and backticks are decoration. Monospace rendering and format-survival are why backticks were chosen as the marker, not the goal; carrying terms into code is Rule 10, encouraged but never syntax-checked; and nothing enforces an entry exists at write time — unanchored artifacts are caught at the recurring review.

questions.question: You add a required column with AddField(default='TBD'). Django's generated SQL adds the column with a database default and then immediately drops that default. Why does this break a rolling deploy?
choices: Old code still running during the rollout inserts rows without naming the column; with the DB default gone, the NOT NULL column rejects those inserts — db_default persists the default and fixes it
The DROP DEFAULT statement takes an exclusive table lock that blocks all reads for the duration of the rollout window
New code reads the Python-side default while the database returns NULL, so the two code versions silently diverge on the value
The migration becomes irreversible once the default is dropped, so a failed deploy strands the schema mid-change
questions.explanation: A rolling deploy has a coexistence window where old and new code hit the same schema, and the old code's INSERT statements simply don't mention the new column — only a database-level default can fill it in. Django drops the DB default because it manages defaults in Python at the ORM layer, which is safe on a single-version system but exactly wrong mid-rollout. db_default (Django 5.0+) persists the default in the schema itself, so the DROP DEFAULT never happens and old-code inserts keep succeeding. Lock contention is a real but separate migration concern, and the failure here is rejected writes, not divergent reads or irreversibility.

questions.question: A host runs an app behind NGINX on 443 (TLS, auth, IP filtering) plus a management tool bound directly to 9443, and the Security Group allows 9443 from 0.0.0.0/0. What is the management tool's actual security posture?
choices: Protected — NGINX runs on the host, so it filters all HTTP traffic entering the instance regardless of port
Exposed to the entire internet — NGINX only governs ports it serves, so 9443 traffic reaches the tool directly with none of NGINX's controls applied
Protected — the Security Group is stateful, so unsolicited inbound connections are blocked automatically
Exposed only to clients that can complete a TLS handshake against the tool's own certificate
questions.explanation: The Security Group and NGINX are gates in series, and NGINX guards only the ports it actually listens on — a port the SG opens that NGINX doesn't proxy is an unguarded door straight to whatever is bound there. Traffic to 9443 never touches NGINX, so its TLS policy, auth, and allow/deny rules simply don't apply; and 'stateful' means allowed inbound connections get their return traffic automatically — it doesn't block connections the rules explicitly permit. TLS on the tool itself encrypts the channel but authenticates nobody. The fix is one of two moves: restrict 9443 at the SG, or route the tool through NGINX — never leave an open port pointing at an unguarded service.

questions.question: A table of editable rows renders with rows.map((r, i) => <Row key={i} />). A user deletes the first row — and text they had typed into the second row's input now appears attached to the first row's data. What is the underlying mechanism?
choices: The delete used splice on the array already in state, mutating it in place, so React could not detect which row actually changed
React batched the delete with the pending input update, so both landed in one commit and the DOM patches were applied to the wrong nodes

key is React's identity contract across re-renders; with index keys every row's identity shifts after a delete, so React matches the old DOM — and its state — to the wrong data rows. The fix is a stable ID from the data
Inputs holding their own value are uncontrolled, violating the single-source-of-truth rule; converting them to controlled components makes the choice of key irrelevant
questions.explanation: React reconciles lists by key — it is the only signal saying which rendered item corresponds to which data item across renders. With key={index}, identity is positional: after deleting row 0, the old row-1 DOM (including whatever the user typed) is matched to the data that shifted into position 0. A stable ID from the data (a DB primary key) keeps identity attached to the item, not the slot. Mutating state in place produces a different symptom — the UI failing to update at all; batching only decides when a re-render happens, not how items are matched; and controlled inputs would merely mask the symptom while React kept reusing the wrong component instances and their state.

questions.question: A vote view increments the chosen row with F('votes') + 1, then returns HttpResponseRedirect(reverse('polls:results', ...)) instead of rendering the results template directly. What failure does the redirect prevent?
choices: Reading a stale vote count: within the same request the F() increment is not yet visible, so rendering directly would show the pre-vote total

Double submission: if the POST itself rendered the final page, refresh or the back button would re-send the POST and record the vote twice; redirecting makes the user's last navigation a harmless, repeatable GET
Leaking the submitted form fields into the URL, since a directly rendered response carries the POST body into the address bar
An uncacheable results page: browsers never cache responses to POST, so a redirect to a GET is required before the page can be cached
questions.explanation: This is the POST/Redirect/GET pattern: a non-idempotent request must never be the page the user ends up on. If the POST returned the results HTML, the browser's current history entry would be the POST itself — refresh and back-button navigation would silently resubmit it and duplicate the write. Redirecting leaves the user on a GET whose repetition is harmless. The staleness worry is unfounded — a request sees its own UPDATE, so a direct render would show the new count; the POST body never appears in the URL either way; and while POST responses are indeed rarely cacheable, cacheability is a side benefit, not the correctness problem this pattern exists to solve.

questions.question: During an incident, every target in an ALB target group starts failing its health checks — yet requests keep flowing to the broken targets and the "traffic is being served" dashboard stays green. What ALB behavior explains this, and what is the monitoring lesson?
choices: Connection draining: existing connections are allowed to finish for deregistration_delay (default 300s), so traffic tails off slowly rather than stopping

Fail-open: when every target in a group is unhealthy, the ALB routes to all of them anyway — a struggling target beats no target — so request volume is not proof of health; alarm on UnHealthyHostCount instead
Cross-zone load balancing: the load balancer nodes redistribute traffic to healthy targets in other Availability Zones, keeping total request volume constant
Health checks only gate the registration of new targets; targets already registered keep receiving traffic regardless of their check results
questions.explanation: The ALB fails open: health checks normally pull a failing target out of rotation, but when the entire group is unhealthy there is nothing left to prefer, so the ALB deliberately routes to all targets — a degraded backend may still serve some requests, while routing to nothing serves none. The operational consequence is that "requests are flowing" can be true while every backend is broken, so dashboards must alarm on health-check state (UnHealthyHostCount) and error rates, never on traffic volume. Draining applies to targets being deliberately deregistered, cross-zone balancing only helps if healthy targets exist somewhere, and under normal conditions health checks absolutely do gate routing for registered targets.

questions.question: To run three coding agents in parallel on one machine, you weigh (a) three separate clones of the repo against (b) three linked worktrees of one repo. Hard requirement: an agent's commit must be reviewable from your main checkout the moment it is made. What is the architectural argument for worktrees?
choices: Separate clones would share .git/HEAD, so a checkout in one agent's clone would silently move the other agents onto its branch
Worktrees give each agent a private ref namespace, so their feature branches cannot collide with yours during review
Worktrees are registered with the remote as a unit, so CI sees all three agents' branches from a single push

Linked worktrees share one object store and ref namespace behind separate working trees, HEADs, and indexes — a commit made at any desk is instantly visible from every other with no push, fetch, or remote round-trip; clones would need a fetch cycle before every review
questions.explanation: A linked worktree is a second desk in front of the same filing cabinet: files, HEAD, and index are per-worktree (agents cannot race each other's checkouts), while objects and refs are shared (a commit made in any worktree is immediately visible from the main one — git log --all and git diff main..feature/x work with zero synchronization). Clones isolate just as well but sever the shared store: every review would need a push from the agent's clone and a fetch into yours. The distractors invert the model — clones share nothing (each has its own HEAD, which is exactly the single-worktree race worktrees were built to fix), worktree refs are shared rather than private, and worktrees are local-only metadata that never reach the remote or CI.

questions.question: A DocumentAttachment table uses a GenericForeignKey — a content_type FK plus a plain object_id column — so one table can attach documents to any model with no schema change per new target. What integrity cost does this design accept, and where must it be repaid?
choices: object_id carries no database FK constraint, so deleting a target row leaves attachment rows dangling; the DB cannot cascade, and cleanup must be reimplemented in application code — e.g. a pre_delete receiver wired for every allowed target model
ContentType rows must be created by hand for each new model, so a forgotten row makes attachments to that model fail at runtime
Every new attachable model requires a migration to widen object_id to the new model's primary-key type
limit_choices_to on the content_type FK is enforced by the database on every insert, so the cost is write throughput rather than integrity
questions.explanation: A GFK trades referential integrity for schema flexibility: because object_id is a plain value column, the database has no idea the link exists — no cascade, no PROTECT, no orphan prevention. That guarantee doesn't disappear; it moves into code. And since deletes arrive from many paths (instance deletes, queryset deletes, FK cascades, admin actions), the robust repayment is a pre_delete signal receiver registered for every model in the attachment registry — a property of the models themselves rather than of each delete path. The distractors invert the design's facts: Django auto-creates ContentType rows at migrate time, object_id keeps one fixed type precisely so new targets need no migration, and limit_choices_to is evaluated only in forms and the admin — it enforces nothing at the database or API layer.

questions.question: A product owner starts embedding each story's full Given/When/Then acceptance criteria in the card itself, "so developers have everything up front." Judged against the 3Cs, what does this practice actually destroy?
choices: Nothing — it strengthens the story by making it Testable from day one, which is the T in INVEST

The card exists as a promise for a conversation; pre-answering the Confirmation on the card skips the conversation where the requirement's detail is meant to emerge, and freezes scope the team was supposed to negotiate — the AC belong to the Confirmation step, written after the discussion
It breaks Independent: acceptance criteria written up front create ordering dependencies between the stories in a sprint
It invalidates estimation, because a story with attached AC can no longer be sized until the criteria are removed
questions.explanation: In the 3Cs model the card is deliberately not the requirement — it is just enough text to identify the story and promise the Conversation, which is where the detail actually lives. Writing final AC on the card pre-answers that conversation, which is precisely the practice the format exists to protect: the story stops being Negotiable, and the Confirmation loses its role as the output of shared discovery (Three Amigos, Example Mapping) and becomes one author's upfront spec. Testability isn't the win here — INVEST's T asks that the outcome be observable, not that Gherkin be drafted before anyone talks. AC don't create inter-story dependencies, and estimation if anything gets easier with more detail — the casualty is negotiation and discovery, not sizing.

questions.question: A DRF ModelViewSet must turn DELETE /api/orders/{id}/ into a soft delete — set archived=True instead of removing the row. DRF splits every write action into an HTTP handler (destroy) and a one-line work hook (perform_destroy). Which override is correct, and why?
choices: Override destroy() and skip self.get_object() — resolving the full object is unnecessary when only one flag changes, and skipping it saves a query
Override the serializer's to_representation to hide archived rows — deletion semantics belong in the JSON layer so every view inherits them
Add @action(detail=True, methods=['delete'], url_path='archive') and leave destroy untouched, so clients opt into soft deletion explicitly
Override perform_destroy(instance) to archive instead of delete — it swaps what deletion means while DRF's destroy keeps the URL resolution, the get_object() 404 contract, and the 204 response
questions.explanation: The handler/hook split is a layering seam: destroy owns the HTTP contract (resolve the pk, 404 on unknown ids, return 204 No Content), while perform_destroy owns the single domain decision of what "delete" means. Soft deletion changes only the latter, so overriding the hook customizes the semantics and inherits the whole contract for free — the same split (create/perform_create, update/perform_update) holds across every write action. Overriding destroy while skipping get_object() is the classic gotcha: unknown ids flow past the 404 check and silently no-op. to_representation shapes output rows and cannot intercept a DELETE; and a separate /archive/ action changes the public API surface when the requirement was to redefine the resource's own DELETE.

questions.question: A story's acceptance criterion reads: "The backend caches the result in Redis for 60 seconds." It is binary and mechanically verifiable — yet it is flagged as an anti-pattern. What is the defect?
choices: It is not measurable enough: the criterion should also pin the Redis eviction policy and memory ceiling to be fully testable
Caching concerns are non-functional, so the statement belongs in the team's Definition of Done rather than in story-level AC

It specifies how instead of what: an AC is a contract on observable behavior, so it should state the user-visible guarantee — e.g. repeated identical searches within 60 seconds return consistent results in under 50 ms — and leave the mechanism to design docs
The format is wrong: a caching rule involves a trigger and an outcome, so it must be rewritten as a Given/When/Then scenario to be automatable
questions.explanation: AC describe what the system does from the outside — what a tester, PO, or customer would recognize as "the thing working" — never how it is built. "Caches in Redis for 60s" welds the story to one design: it cannot be verified without inspecting internals, it forbids equally valid implementations (in-process cache, CDN, precomputation), and it silently goes stale the day the design changes. Restated as an observable guarantee — a consistency window plus a latency threshold — the criterion survives any implementation and stays testable at the system boundary. Pinning eviction policy digs even deeper into implementation; the DoD holds team-wide gates that apply to every story, not story-specific behavior; and checklist-vs-Gherkin is orthogonal — the defect is the content, not the format.

questions.question: You delete legacy_ref — a NOT NULL column with no default — from the model, and the RemoveField migration is correctly staged post-deploy. Yet during the rollout, as soon as new-code servers come up, their INSERTs start failing. Why?
choices: RemoveField acquires an exclusive table lock that blocks concurrent inserts for the duration of the rollout window
Django's runtime model state diverges from the schema, so the ORM raises as soon as it encounters a column it no longer knows about

The new code's INSERTs no longer name legacy_ref, but the column still exists until the post-deploy drop — NOT NULL with no default rejects those writes; a pre-deploy step must first make the column nullable or give it a db_default
The staging is inverted: destructive operations must run pre-deploy so that both code versions see the same schema throughout the rollout
questions.explanation: The remove side of the coexistence window is symmetric to the add side: the moment the field leaves the model, Django stops listing it in INSERT statements — and the column is deliberately still in the schema, because the drop is staged after the old code is gone. A NOT NULL column with no default rejects any insert that doesn't name it, so the new code breaks against a column only the old code still fills. Field removal is therefore inherently two-phase: a pre-deploy AlterField making the column nullable (or persisting a db_default), then the post-deploy RemoveField — django-syzygy generates that pre-deploy half automatically; with django-safemigrate you stage it yourself. No lock is involved since the drop hasn't run yet; the ORM never introspects the schema at runtime; and moving destructive drops pre-deploy would break the old code instead — the mirror-image failure.

questions.question: "Customer" means one thing to Sales and another to Support, and specs keep tripping over it. A lead proposes a single company-wide definition to end the ambiguity. Why do DDD and CAS reject that move, and what do they prescribe instead?
choices: Total unification of a large domain's model is not feasible or cost-effective — a forced global definition matches nobody's real usage and quietly gets ignored; instead, fence the polysemy: two Contexts, each owning its own coherent definition, with the divergence documented in their Relationships
One definition is correct, but it must be owned by the larger of the two departments, with the other Context importing it read-only
Formal definitions are the mistake: concrete usage examples inside each story remove ambiguity without any dictionary maintenance
Retire the ambiguous word entirely and mint two newly invented terms to be used company-wide in speech, specs, and code
questions.explanation: DDD's central admission — the reason Bounded Contexts are its central pattern — is that one model for a whole organization is neither feasible nor cost-effective: language boundaries follow human culture, and both departments' meanings of "Customer" are correct within their own context. A forced company-wide definition produces the worst outcome — a term nobody actually uses — so the drift goes back underground where it is most expensive. The prescription is to stop fighting polysemy and fence it: one Context per coherent vocabulary, each owning its own Dictionary entry, with the relationship stated explicitly so cross-context Stories know to disambiguate (`term[Context]`). Imposing the bigger department's definition is unification wearing sharing clothes; examples without definitions leave the drift latent; and minting invented vocabulary recreates the same nobody-uses-it failure with extra confusion.

questions.question: A colleague built and applied a Terraform configuration from their laptop. You clone the repo, use the same AWS account and profile, run terraform init and then terraform plan — and the plan proposes to create every resource in the config, even though they all already exist and are serving traffic. What explains this, and what is the structural fix?
choices: The state file — Terraform's mapping between config and real resources — was rightly never committed and lives only on the colleague's laptop; without it Terraform cannot distinguish "doesn't exist yet" from "exists and is managed by me". The fix is a remote backend (e.g. S3), which shares state and adds locking against concurrent applies
terraform init re-downloaded newer provider plugins, and that version drift makes existing resources unrecognizable to the planner; pinning versions in required_providers reconciles the plan
terraform plan works offline against the configuration alone and never queries the live API — only apply contacts AWS, so only apply would discover the existing resources
Terraform matches infrastructure to configuration by resource local name, and the colleague used different block names; renaming the resource blocks to match would reconcile the plan
questions.explanation: plan compares three things: the config (desired), the state (what Terraform last knew), and reality — but it refreshes reality only for resources recorded in state. With no state file present, nothing is tracked, so every resource looks like it needs creating; applying would attempt duplicates or collide on names. The state file is also the reason the fix is a backend rather than git: state can contain secrets in plaintext, so committing it is wrong — a remote backend gives shared source-of-truth state, access control, and locking so two applies cannot corrupt it concurrently. The distractors misplace the mechanism: provider version drift doesn't orphan resources (tracking lives in state, not in the plugin), plan absolutely does query the live API for refresh — just only for what state lists — and matching is by the IDs recorded in state, not by config block names.

questions.question: A teammate tunes LightGBM by grid-searching learning_rate ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.1} × n_estimators ∈ {200, 1000, 5000} as independent dials — nine expensive fits. The tuning playbook instead says: fix the learning rate, set n_estimators as a huge ceiling, and let early stopping choose. What understanding is the grid missing?
choices: learning_rate and n_estimators are the step size and step count of one gradient-descent budget — halve one and you roughly double the other for the same training loss. The grid mostly re-tests equivalent budgets and compares configs at arbitrary tree counts; with a fixed rate, a high ceiling, and early stopping, each config is judged at its own validation minimum (best_iteration_), the honest value of n_estimators
In leaf-wise trees the number of boosting rounds is determined by num_leaves, so n_estimators is not a real hyperparameter and only the learning rate needed searching
More trees monotonically improve accuracy, so n_estimators should simply be set to the maximum affordable and only learning_rate belongs in the search
Grid search overfits the validation set whenever two parameters interact; the playbook's point is that random search must replace grids for coupled parameters
questions.explanation: The two dials are Stage-⑤ gradient descent's η and its number of steps — one budget, not two independent knobs. The validation curve over boosting rounds has a minimum: before it the model is still descending, past it every extra tree is pure overfit. So the right tree count is a property of the data at a given learning rate, best discovered by early stopping (then retraining at best_iteration_), not guessed from a grid — and a grid that fixes n_estimators per cell compares some configs before their minimum and others past it, an unfair comparison throughout. The distractors confuse the axes: num_leaves is per-tree capacity, orthogonal to how many trees are boosted; accuracy is not monotone in tree count precisely because of the post-minimum overfit; and random-vs-grid search is a separate debate — the defect here is treating a coupled pair as independent, which no search geometry fixes.

questions.question: The step definition for "Given a lesson exists in a module locked for review" can be implemented two ways: script the UI (log in, click through the lesson form, lock the module) or make two authenticated API calls (create-lesson, then lock-module). The BDD guidance firmly picks the API — for a reason beyond speed. Which?
choices: Gherkin forbids actions inside Given steps, and UI clicks are actions; API calls keep the step syntactically a precondition

A Given is scaffolding, not behaviour under test. Building preconditions through screens creates false dependencies: an unrelated redesign of a page the scenario merely passes through breaks every scenario that used it for setup. State is set up through the API, the UI is exercised only by the behaviour the scenario actually specifies — and a precondition with no API to build it is a finding to flag, not a reason to click through
UI-driven setup breaks scenario isolation, because browser state persists between scenarios while API calls are stateless
Setup through the UI makes the scenario imperative, and imperative scenarios cannot be matched by step-definition patterns
questions.explanation: Declarative style evicts the "how" from scenarios into step definitions — and inside step definitions the same layering discipline continues: preconditions get built at the cheapest reliable layer, which is the API. The architectural argument is about coupling, not speed: a scenario that clicks through the lesson form to set up state now depends on that form's markup, so any redesign of it breaks scenarios whose subject is something else entirely — false dependencies that make the suite brittle and failures misleading. And when no API exists to build a precondition, the guidance treats that as a discovery (a missing or test-only endpoint to add) rather than a dead end. The distractors misattribute the rule: Gherkin does not police what code a step executes; isolation is the harness's job (fresh browser context and API-created data per scenario) regardless of how setup happens; and an imperative scenario matches step definitions just fine — its defect is brittleness as documentation, a different failure than this one.

questions.question: An AttachmentSerializer must output an invoice_number key for rows with entity_type == 'invoice', and for every other row the key must be absent from the JSON — not null. The developer searches for a way to declare the field "only for invoice rows" and finds none. What constraint are they hitting, and what is the sanctioned pattern?
choices: Serializers bind per queryset, not per row; the fix is two serializer classes with get_serializer_class() switching between them
Override get_fields() to inspect the instance and drop the field — it is DRF's per-row hook for shaping output
DRF fields accept a callable for required, so required=lambda obj: obj.entity_type == 'invoice' conditionally includes the field

Serializer fields are class-level declarations evaluated once at import — the field set cannot vary per row. The pattern is add-then-strip: declare a SerializerMethodField whose getter returns None for non-invoice rows, then override to_representation to call super() first and pop the keys that don't apply, so each entity_type gets a typed shape with no null noise
questions.explanation: Declaration and per-row shaping live at two different layers. Fields are defined on the class and fixed at import time, so "a field for some rows only" is unexpressible there; per-row divergence belongs in to_representation, the last hook before JSON encoding, where the built dict can be mutated per instance. The idiom composes the two: the method field computes the value for every row (returning None where inapplicable), and to_representation strips the inapplicable keys — with the usual caveat that a getter touching related rows on a list endpoint invites N+1 queries. The distractors reach for hooks that operate at the wrong granularity: get_serializer_class() picks one class per request, and in a many=True response a single child serializer instance handles every row, so neither it nor get_fields() (which runs per serializer instantiation, not per object) can vary shape row-by-row; and required takes no callable — it governs input validation, not output shape, so it is doubly wrong for this job.

questions.question: LightGBM special-cases objective='quantile' with IsRenewTreeOutput() = true: after each tree's structure is chosen, every leaf value is overwritten with the α-percentile of the residuals that landed in that leaf. The standard Newton leaf value w* = −ΣG/(ΣH+λ) works fine for L2 — why can it not produce a calibrated quantile here?
choices: Pinball loss is non-convex, so the Newton step can diverge; the percentile overwrite is a safeguard against oscillation
Trees can only output the mean of their training targets, so quantile targeting requires changing the tree-growing algorithm itself — which the renewal step does

Differentiating pinball loss yields a piecewise-constant gradient — (1−α) or −α, a direction with no magnitude — and a true second derivative of zero, for which LightGBM substitutes a placeholder h = 1 just to keep the solver running. The Newton step then reduces to a fixed per-leaf nudge that knows which way to move but not how far, so it cannot calibrate onto the α-quantile; the labour is split — gradient signs shape the tree, the residual percentile sets what each leaf predicts
With the true hessian of zero, ΣH+λ collapses to just λ and leaf values explode in magnitude; renewal exists to cap them
questions.explanation: The hinge of GBDT is that everything after split-finding depends on the loss only through g and h. For L2, g = ŷ − y is proportional to the error, so the Newton value −ΣG/(ΣH+λ) lands on roughly the mean residual — magnitude information flows straight into the leaf. Pinball loss breaks that channel: its gradient encodes only which side of the point you're on, scaled by α versus 1−α, and its curvature is zero everywhere (undefined at the kink), so the h = 1 is a fiction. Direction without magnitude cannot converge onto a specific percentile — hence the two-phase design where gradients pick the splits and a weighted percentile of residuals sets each leaf's output. The distractors each miss the mechanism: pinball loss is convex (an asymmetric V), just not smooth; the tree-growing machinery is deliberately unchanged — only leaf values are renewed, which is the elegance of the fix; and the λ-explosion never arises precisely because the placeholder hessian is 1, not the true 0 — renewal replaces values with the right statistic rather than capping wrong ones.

questions.question: Agent 1 is working in slot ../proj-agent1 with feature/task-1 checked out. To review its work you run git worktree add ../review feature/task-1 — and git refuses: the branch is already checked out elsewhere. What failure is this rule preventing, and what should you do instead?
choices: Two checkouts of one branch would fork the shared object store, duplicating every blob the branch touches until the stores are reconciled
The rule protects the remote: pushes from two worktrees on the same branch would create divergent refs on origin

Worktrees share a single ref namespace but each has its own HEAD, index, and files. With one branch checked out at two desks, a commit made at either silently moves the branch tip under the other, leaving its working tree and index based on a commit that is no longer the branch head — the same class of silent desync worktrees exist to fix. Review needs no checkout anyway: refs and objects are shared, so git log and git diff main..feature/task-1 work from the main desk; use --detach for a read-only checkout of the files
Each branch's reflog accepts writes from only one worktree, so a second checkout would corrupt the shared reflog
questions.explanation: The worktree model splits .git into shared parts (objects, refs, config) and per-worktree parts (HEAD, index, working files). That split is exactly why a branch may live in only one worktree: the branch pointer is shared while the checked-out files are not, so two desks on one branch would race each other's commits — the mirror image of the shared-.git/HEAD race that motivated worktrees in the first place, which is why it's a safety check (bypassable with --force only knowingly). The refusal also points at the better workflow: because commits and refs are visible from every worktree instantly, reviewing an agent's branch requires no checkout at all — log, diff, and even merging from the main desk all work without touching the agent's slot; --detach covers the rare case where you need the files themselves. The distractors contradict the architecture: the object store is content-addressed, append-only, and shared — nothing forks; worktrees are local-only metadata that never reach origin or CI; and reflogs are per-ref bookkeeping, not a locking mechanism.

questions.question: A team migrates from XGBoost, where max_depth=6 was their main overfitting control, to LightGBM. They carry max_depth=6 over, leave num_leaves at its default 31, and still overfit. The tuning guidance says capacity in LightGBM is governed by num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf, with max_depth demoted to a 'safety rail'. What about leaf-wise growth changes which dial matters?
choices: Level-wise trees expand the whole frontier floor by floor, so depth ≈ capacity and a depth cap is a real capacity dial. Leaf-wise growth instead always splits the single best-gain leaf in the whole tree, producing asymmetric trees whose depth is emergent — capacity is the leaf count, and the characteristic overfit is deep, thin branches chasing tiny pockets of residual noise. num_leaves caps total capacity and min_data_in_leaf makes those noise pockets unreachable; a depth cap constrains the wrong dimension of an asymmetric tree

num_leaves and max_depth are mutually exclusive in LightGBM: setting both causes the library to ignore both and fall back to unconstrained growth, which is why carrying max_depth over silently removed all capacity control

Leaf-wise trees are systematically shallower than level-wise trees of equal accuracy, so a depth-6 cap never binds; the overfitting comes from histogram binning noise, which min_data_in_leaf exists to smooth out

Histograms quantize every feature into at most 255 bins, blurring split thresholds so that depth no longer correlates with model complexity; min_data_in_leaf compensates by forcing more rows through each blurred split
questions.explanation: The right dial follows the growth strategy. Level-wise growth finishes every node at one depth before descending, so a depth-d tree has a predictable symmetric shape — capping depth caps capacity. Leaf-wise growth spends its split budget wherever gain is highest, growing deep exactly where residuals still pay; its failure mode is a few far-down leaves memorizing noise, which is why the brake is a per-leaf row floor (min_data_in_leaf) plus a total leaf cap (num_leaves), not a depth ceiling the asymmetric shape mostly ignores. There is also a silent interaction worth knowing: when both are set, the smaller of num_leaves and 2^max_depth rules with no warning — here 31 < 2^6 = 64, so the carried-over depth cap was not even the binding constraint. The distractors invent mechanics: setting both dials never disables them (the tighter one wins silently); leaf-wise trees grow deeper, not shallower, where it pays; and histogram binning is a split-finding speed trick whose accuracy cost is famously near zero — it is unrelated to capacity control.

questions.question: You point boto3 at the local MinIO container (endpoint_url='http://minio:9000'), and every S3 call fails with a connection error mentioning a host named user-uploads.minio. The identical code works against real AWS. What design difference explains the mangled hostname, and what is the fix?
choices: boto3 defaults to virtual-hosted-style addressing, which encodes the bucket in the hostname (bucket.s3.region.amazonaws.com) — a scheme that works on AWS only because AWS operates DNS for every bucket subdomain. Against a custom endpoint, user-uploads.minio resolves to nothing. Path-style addressing keeps the host fixed and carries the bucket in the URL path (host/bucket/key), which works against any endpoint: set addressing_style 'path' in the client's Config

MinIO requires buckets to exist before any call, and the odd hostname is boto3's fallback lookup for a missing bucket; running the mc mb setup step so user-uploads exists makes the client revert to normal addressing

The endpoint_url must include the bucket (http://minio:9000/user-uploads) because MinIO, unlike AWS, cannot infer the bucket from credentials; without it boto3 guesses by prepending the bucket to the host
Docker's embedded DNS refuses dotted service names; adding a network alias 'user-uploads.minio' to the MinIO service resolves the hostname and fixes the calls without touching client configuration
questions.explanation: S3 has two URL shapes, and the failure is the gap between them. Virtual-hosted style turns every bucket into a DNS name — viable when Amazon runs the DNS for *.s3.region.amazonaws.com, impossible for an arbitrary endpoint like a compose-stack container. Path-style exists for exactly this case: one fixed host, bucket in the path, so the same client works against any S3-compatible server. That is why the missing addressing_style is called the single most common MinIO-from-SDK mistake — the storage code is correct, the addressing contract is not. The distractors confuse layers: a genuinely missing bucket produces an S3-level NoSuchBucket 404 after a successful connection, never a DNS failure, and bucket existence has no effect on URL formation; endpoint_url is a base host by contract — the SDK composes the bucket into host or path according to the addressing style, and stuffing the bucket into the endpoint fights that machinery; and a Docker network alias can paper over one bucket's hostname, but it hand-rebuilds AWS's per-bucket DNS for every bucket you ever create — re-implementing the very requirement path-style removes.

questions.question: A BDD suite has 45 Gherkin scenarios, all executed through the browser: 5 happy paths and 40 validation, permission, and limit sad paths. CI takes 50 minutes and flakes weekly. A teammate proposes deleting the sad-path scenarios and rewriting them as plain unit tests. What does the guidance actually prescribe?
choices: Keep all 45 in the browser and parallelize CI instead: acceptance scenarios are end-to-end by definition, and moving any of them off the UI layer downgrades them from acceptance tests to integration tests

Push scenarios down the pyramid without abandoning the discipline: acceptance scenarios are not chained to the top layer. Keep the happy path in the browser — one scenario per slice, proving the whole thing hangs together — and run the sad paths as the same Gherkin, at the API layer: no browser, the same specification-and-verification role, a fraction of the cost and flake
Accept the proposal: Gherkin's ceremony is only justified for the happy paths stakeholders actually read, and validation rules are implementation detail best covered by developer-facing unit tests

Collapse the 40 sad paths into a few Scenario Outlines: one scenario template with a large Examples table per rule family cuts scenario setup overhead, keeping full browser coverage at a fraction of the runtime
questions.explanation: The pyramid rule and the BDD discipline are orthogonal, and the guidance keeps both: 'there's technically no need to write acceptance tests at the highest level — push your tests as far down the test pyramid as you can.' Gherkin's value is that the scenarios are the specification — business-readable, and drift fails the build — and that property does not depend on which layer executes the steps. Running sad paths against the API keeps every rule inside the living documentation while removing the browser's cost and flakiness; the single UI happy path still proves the slice integrates end to end. The distractors each sacrifice one half: 'acceptance means E2E' is exactly the misconception the guidance rejects; rewriting rules as unit tests silently deletes them from the living documentation, so the specification can drift from the system again without failing anything; and Scenario Outline through the UI is a named anti-pattern — each Examples row still drives the full browser flow, so the table multiplies runtime instead of cutting it.

questions.question: Migrating from a single EC2 host (NGINX at the edge) to ECS behind an ALB, a team copies their VPN-only block for /admin — allow 10.8.0.0/24; deny all; — into the per-task NGINX config. After cutover, every /admin request is denied, including from the VPN. Why, and where must the rule live now?
choices: The task's security group now admits traffic only from the ALB's security group, which rewrites the packet source to the ALB's address; adding the VPN CIDR to the task security group restores the original source IP

The ALB terminates TLS, so the per-task NGINX receives plain HTTP — and location-level allow/deny directives are only evaluated on TLS-terminated server blocks; re-terminating TLS at the task's NGINX re-enables the rules

In the old topology NGINX was the edge, so each connection's source address was the real client and the allowlist worked on it. Behind an ALB, the per-task NGINX sees the load balancer's IP on every connection: 10.8.0.0/24 never matches, so deny all catches everyone — VPN included. IP filtering must move to the layer that still sees the client: an ALB listener rule with a source_ip condition (the ALB now plays the L7-edge role), or NGINX trusting X-Forwarded-For from the ALB

Cross-zone load balancing rotates requests across ALB nodes whose addresses change over time, so any IP-based allowlist behind an ALB is inherently unstable; the fix is fronting the service with a Network Load Balancer, whose static IPs can be allowlisted
questions.explanation: The rule didn't break — its input did. NGINX allow/deny evaluates the TCP connection's source address, and moving NGINX from the edge to behind a proxy changes what that address is: the ALB opens its own connections to the task, so every request arrives 'from' the ALB. The general principle: L7 access control must live wherever the real client identity is visible — at the new edge (ALB listener rules with source_ip conditions), or downstream only via an explicitly trusted header chain (X-Forwarded-For from a proxy you control). That is exactly why, on the ECS path, VPN restrictions are ALB rules rather than task-level nginx deny blocks. The distractors attribute the failure to the wrong layers: security groups admit or drop packets but never rewrite source addresses — and if the SG were blocking, requests would time out rather than get denied responses; TLS termination changes what NGINX decrypts, not whether location rules run — allow/deny works fine on plain HTTP; and rotating node IPs are why clients use the ALB's DNS name, irrelevant to how NGINX evaluates an inbound connection's source.

questions.question: A team deploys a new version by deregistering the old ECS tasks from the ALB target group and stopping them immediately. Users report dropped connections and 502s during every deploy — yet health checks stay green throughout. Which mechanism did the team bypass, and what is the graceful pattern?
choices: The health-check interval (30 s) times the unhealthy threshold (2) means the ALB needs up to a minute to notice a stopped task and keeps routing to it; lowering the interval to 5 s and the threshold to 1 makes deploys near-seamless without other changes

Deregistration puts a target into a draining state: the ALB stops sending it new requests but lets in-flight ones finish, for up to deregistration_delay (default 300 s). Stopping the process immediately kills exactly those live connections — the draining window exists so old tasks can finish the work they hold. Graceful deploys stop a target only after draining completes; the lesson is that shutdown is a two-phase act — stop accepting new work, then finish the work in hand

With cross-zone load balancing enabled (the ALB default), every node routes to every target, so a deregistered task keeps receiving requests from nodes in other zones until their target lists converge; disabling cross-zone makes deregistration take effect zone-locally and instantly

Clients cache the ALB's DNS record for its 60-second TTL, so requests keep arriving at node IPs that still hold connections to the old tasks; fronting the ALB with a Route 53 alias record eliminates the client-side caching window
questions.explanation: The failure sits at the connection-lifecycle layer, not the health layer. Health checks answer 'should NEW requests go to this target?' — they say nothing about requests already in flight. Deregistration likewise governs new traffic, and provides deregistration_delay precisely so the old traffic can complete: that is connection draining, the mechanism that makes rolling deploys invisible to users. Killing the process the moment deregistration starts turns every in-flight request into a reset connection, and no health-check tuning can help because health was never the problem — the green checks throughout were the tell. Orchestrators like ECS honour the draining window automatically; deregister-then-kill by hand re-creates the failure. The distractors blame real mechanisms for the wrong failure: faster health checks only shrink detection time for targets that fail, which these didn't; cross-zone balancing changes which nodes route to which targets, but draining state applies across all nodes either way; and DNS TTL governs how clients find ALB nodes, not how the ALB manages its own server-side connections to targets.

questions.question: During Dictionary drafting, a teammate proposes adding every noun in the Spec File — 'page', 'button', 'filter', 'list', roughly sixty entries — arguing that a complete glossary can only help. CAS's inclusion bar (ambiguity, domain weight, or recurrence) keeps most of those out. What makes a deliberately small Dictionary load-bearing rather than stingy?
choices: Sixty entries make the Context block long, and long markdown documents are painful to edit and review; the framework keeps Dictionaries small so that definition edits stay reviewable as clean per-term diffs

Everyday UI words belong in a separate UI Context with its own Dictionary; the mistake is not listing them but putting them in a business Context, which breaks the one-vocabulary-per-Context invariant

Highlighting is a signal, and the inclusion bar keeps it honest. Every defined term must be backticked at every dictionary-sense use, so each entry taxes all future Stories and AC — and a Dictionary full of everyday words makes backticks so common they stop meaning 'this word carries a checked, shared definition'. Rule 9's grep-based propagation degrades the same way: re-review sets balloon with incidental matches. Terms earn entries via ambiguity, domain weight, or recurrence; doubtful ones stay out and the pruning pass decides
A large Dictionary makes AI-assisted drafting unreliable: generation quality drops as the terminology context grows, so the framework keeps Dictionaries small enough to fit inside a drafting prompt
questions.explanation: The Dictionary is not documentation for completeness' sake — it is an index of exactly the words where misunderstanding is plausible and costly. Its value comes from precision: when a reader hits a backticked term, that markup must reliably mean 'stop — this has a checked definition'. Sixty everyday nouns destroy the property twice over: readers learn to skim past backticks (signal dilution), and a definition change to any real term greps into a haystack of incidental matches, making Rule 9's mechanical propagation noisy exactly where it must be trusted. That is why the framework calls the inclusion bar its immune system and pairs it with recurring pruning — zero citations removes an entry, one citation gets judged, favouring lean. The distractors reach for adjacent but non-load-bearing concerns: per-term sections do give clean diffs, but that argues for the format, not the size; a UI Context would merely relocate the bloat — the words still fail the earn-your-entry test wherever they live; and prompt-size ergonomics is no framework concern — the economics being protected are those of the human reading signal.

questions.question: A Django service wraps an upload flow in transaction.atomic: it calls storage.save() to push the file to S3, creates the Attachment row, and then a later validation step raises. The row is rolled back — but the object is still in the bucket, orphaned. A teammate proposes 'moving storage.save() deeper inside the atomic block so it joins the transaction.' Why can't that work, and what is the honest pattern?
choices: The mistake is calling storage.save() manually: assigning the upload to the model's FileField and letting model.save() persist both makes Django coordinate the file write with the row write inside the transaction

Nested atomic blocks create savepoints, and a savepoint taken before storage.save() lets the rollback restore both the row and the file; the code just needs the storage call wrapped in its own inner atomic block

transaction.atomic governs exactly one system: the database connection. S3 does not participate in that transaction — wherever the call sits inside the block, a rollback cannot un-PUT an object, because the guarantee never extended past the DB. Side effects on external systems need explicit compensation: keep the blob write and the row write adjacent, and on failure delete the stored object in an except branch — write, then compensate — or defer the external write until after commit. The design habit: know which operations are inside the transactional boundary and which only look like they are
Enabling bucket versioning dissolves the problem: the orphaned PUT becomes a non-current version that lifecycle rules expire, giving storage the same all-or-nothing semantics the database provides
questions.explanation: A transaction is a contract with one resource manager — here, the database. Everything inside atomic is provisional until commit because the database itself holds the machinery (undo logs, savepoints) to revoke it. An HTTP PUT to an object store carries no such machinery: the moment it returns, the object exists, and your connection's eventual COMMIT or ROLLBACK is invisible to S3. Placement inside the block is therefore cosmetic — this is the distributed-transaction boundary, and pretending a code block spans it is how orphaned blobs (or worse, committed rows pointing at never-written files) are born. Honest patterns acknowledge the two systems: compensate on failure — a try/except that deletes the stored object, a saga in miniature — or reorder so the external write happens only once the DB outcome is known (transaction.on_commit is the Django hook for the latter). Tests share the blind spot: TestCase rolls back DB writes, but storage writes persist unless explicitly cleaned. The distractors dress the gap in Django idioms: FileField assignment changes who calls storage, not its transactionality; savepoints are database-internal markers no external system honours; and versioning changes what an orphan looks like — an expiring non-current version is still a write the rollback never undid.

questions.question: OrderDetail fetches /api/orders/{id}/ inside useEffect(..., [id]) and calls setOrder(data) in the .then. QA reports that navigating quickly from order A to order B sometimes shows A's data under B's URL. The author is confused — the effect clearly re-ran for B; B's request is right there in the network tab. What is the mechanism, and the idiomatic fix?
choices: The dependency array is incomplete: the effect reads order via its closure, and with only [id] listed it can act on a stale snapshot; adding order to the dependencies keeps the effect synchronized

React batches state updates, so A's and B's setOrder calls landed in one render pass in arrival order; the updater form setOrder(prev => data) makes each update see the latest state so the later navigation wins

Both effect runs completed their fetches — nothing ever cancelled A's. Each effect run closes over its own id, and its .then stays alive after the component re-renders for B; since network completion order is not render order, A's slower response resolved last and overwrote B's data with setOrder. React's contract for exactly this is cleanup: return a function that flips an ignore flag (or aborts via AbortController); React invokes it before the next effect run and on unmount, so a superseded request's response is discarded the moment it lands. The habit: any async effect must assume it may be stale by the time it resolves, and cleanup is how the next run tells it so
Fetching in response to navigation is an event, not synchronization — move the fetch into the click handler that navigates, where you know exactly which order was chosen, and the race disappears
questions.explanation: The bug lives in the gap between two orderings: React re-runs effects in render order, but the network resolves in its own order, and a .then callback belongs to the render that created it — it fires regardless of how many renders have happened since. So 'the effect re-ran for B' is true and irrelevant: A's promise was still pending, still holding a live closure with a live setOrder, and it landed last. The framework's answer is structural, not clever: the cleanup function is defined to run before the effect's next execution, which makes it the exact hook for invalidating the previous run's pending work — the docs' own ignore-flag pattern, or AbortController to cancel the request outright. The distractors misapply real React facts: the effect never reads order, and adding it to the dependencies would create a set-state-then-re-run loop; batching coalesces updates within one event or render pass, not across independently resolving promises, and the updater form orders state transitions without knowing which request is fresher — freshness is a property of the request, not the state; and 'you might not need an Effect' targets derived state and event side-effects, whereas fetching whatever the current URL demands is genuine external-system synchronization — deep links and the back button never pass through a click handler, and relocating the fetch would not serialize response arrival anyway.

questions.question: A reusable module makes its S3 bucket optional with count = var.bucket_name != "" ? 1 : 0. Its outputs.tf exposes value = aws_s3_bucket.this.arn, and now even callers that DO pass a bucket name fail: 'Because aws_s3_bucket.this has count set, its attributes must be accessed on specific instances.' A teammate proposes deleting the count so the module always creates the bucket. What is the mental model to fix, and the sanctioned pattern?
choices: The output is evaluated before the resource exists in the graph; a bare reference isn't enough for optional resources, so the output needs an explicit depends_on pointing at the bucket
Conditional resources fight the declarative model — the clean design is two modules, with-bucket and without-bucket, and each caller picks one; a module whose contents vary by input is the real smell

count changes the resource's type, not just its quantity: the moment a resource carries count it becomes a list — even at count = 1 — so every reference must select an instance: aws_s3_bucket.this[0].arn. And because that list can be empty, any expression that might evaluate when the bucket doesn't exist needs its own guard: local.create_bucket ? aws_s3_bucket.this[0].arn : "". That shared condition is exactly why it earns a named local — one rule read by the resource, the output, and any sibling resources it gates. Deleting count removes the error by deleting the feature: callers that want no bucket get one anyway. The modern refinement is for_each, whose named instances (this["main"]) avoid positional indexing entirely

The ternary belongs on the argument, not the resource: bucket = var.bucket_name == "" ? null : var.bucket_name tells Terraform not to create the bucket when no name is supplied, keeping the resource address a plain single object
questions.explanation: The error is a type error, not an ordering problem: count re-types the resource from 'one object' to 'a list of objects', and Terraform enforces the new shape everywhere — including references written before count was added, which is why callers who do get a bucket still fail. The complete pattern therefore has two halves: index every reference (this[0]) and guard every reference that can run against the empty list, returning a sentinel like "" so downstream code stays evaluable in both worlds. Naming the condition as a local (create_bucket) is what keeps those halves consistent as the condition spreads to the bucket's versioning, encryption, and policy resources — one line to change, not five. The distractors trade the feature away or misdiagnose: depends_on addresses ordering, but references already create implicit dependencies and the plan never got that far — it failed at addressing; duplicating the module resolves a one-line ternary by forking an entire maintenance surface, when local + count is the documented idiom for one-or-none; and a null argument is not an off switch — Terraform treats it as 'argument unset', which for a required argument is a validation error, never 'skip this resource'. count and for_each are the only cardinality levers a resource has, and for_each's stable keys are the upgrade path when positional [0] starts to churn.

questions.question: A redesign replaces a form-based upload dialog with drag-and-drop. No behavior changed, yet 40 Gherkin scenarios fail — they read like 'When I click the file input / And I select "syllabus-2026.pdf" from the picker / And I click the Upload button'. The team budgets a week to update the specs. What is the actual defect, per BDD's Formulation practice?
choices: The scenarios are imperative: they encode the current UI's mechanics as if the mechanics were the specification, so a purely mechanical change reads as 40 behavioral regressions. Formulation's core style rule is declarative scenarios: the spec states what the actor accomplishes — 'When the Course Author uploads the file "syllabus-2026.pdf"' — and the clicks live in step definitions, the one layer entitled to know the UI's current shape. Rewritten declaratively, the redesign becomes an edit to one step definition, and the feature files — the living documentation — correctly show that no behavior changed. Declarative is not vague: hide the mechanics, keep the data concrete
The steps lack a page-object layer: keep the click-level steps but route every selector through page objects, so the next redesign is absorbed by updating one class instead of 40 files

Each scenario carries several When steps — a known anti-pattern signalling multiple behaviors per scenario; splitting them into single-trigger scenarios would have contained the blast radius to a handful of failures
Forty scenarios through the browser is a test-pyramid violation; re-pointing them at the API layer removes the UI dependency entirely, so no redesign can break them again
questions.explanation: The tell is that the specification changed while the behavior didn't — for an artifact whose whole claim is 'living documentation of behavior', that is the system lying about what happened. Imperative steps are, in the docs' words, so closely tied to the mechanics of the current UI that every UI change forces a spec change; the fix is a division of labor, not better tooling: scenarios own the what (with concrete data, so they can fail meaningfully), step definitions own the how, and a redesign that preserves behavior touches only the second. The week of 'updating specs' becomes minutes of updating one step's implementation. The distractors each relocate the coupling instead of removing it: page objects deduplicate selector code, but the spec text still asserts clicks and pickers that no longer exist — the falsehood is in the language, not the locators; the multiple-When smell is real but is a symptom here — splitting imperative steps yields more, smaller imperative scenarios, every one still UI-coupled; and the pyramid guidance (happy path through the UI, sad paths at the API) optimizes cost, not correctness of expression — imperative scenarios re-pointed at an API would just couple to endpoint mechanics instead, and abandoning UI coverage because the specs were badly written treats the symptom while keeping the disease.

questions.question: A pre_delete receiver on Order detaches its DocumentAttachments; it is wired in AppConfig.ready() and works from the admin, the shell, and API deletes. A cleanup data migration then deletes obsolete orders via apps.get_model('store', 'Order') inside RunPython — and staging ends up with dangling attachment rows: the receiver never fired. Why?
choices: AppConfig.ready() doesn't run for manage.py migrate — only for request-serving processes — so no receiver was connected during the migration run; moving the connect calls to the top of models.py fixes it
Queryset .delete() takes a bulk fast path that skips per-instance signals; the migration should loop and call instance.delete() one row at a time so each fires pre_delete
Signals are deferred until transaction commit, and each migration runs inside its own transaction that the migrate process finalizes after dispatch has already been torn down

Signals dispatch by sender identity, and RunPython never hands you your classes: the apps argument resolves models against the historical snapshot registry — plain reconstructed classes pinned to that migration's point in schema history, distinct objects from the live classes your receiver is connected to. A delete through the snapshot Order is a delete from a different sender, so the wiring never matches; by design, since a migration must stay runnable years later when today's code no longer resembles that snapshot. The honest patterns: make the migration self-contained (delete the attachment rows explicitly in the same RunPython), or do the cleanup operationally through a management command, which uses live classes — service seam, signals, and all
questions.explanation: The mechanism is two Django facts composing: receivers registered with a sender are keyed to a specific class object, and RunPython's apps registry deliberately does not contain your class objects — it rebuilds bare model classes from the migration graph's recorded state, so the code runs against the schema as it was, independent of what models.py says today. That independence is the entire reliability contract of data migrations (they must apply cleanly on a fresh database long after the code has moved on), and its price is that everything attached to your live classes — custom methods, managers' overrides, and signal wiring — is absent. The dangling rows follow directly: the snapshot Order deletes fine, but the sender your receiver listens for was never involved. The right responses respect the boundary rather than fight it: a migration should carry its own cleanup logic inline (idempotent, snapshot-only), or the operation belongs in a management command where live classes — and therefore the single seam and the registry-driven signals — apply. The distractors invent plausible machinery: ready() runs whenever the app registry initializes, management commands included — and module-top wiring is the AppRegistryNotReady trap ready() exists to prevent; queryset deletes are covered — the deletion Collector fetches rows and fires pre_delete for each before the bulk DELETE, which is exactly why admin and shell deletes worked; and lifecycle signals fire inline at delete time — deferral-to-commit describes transaction.on_commit, a separate opt-in hook, not the signal framework.

questions.question: A delivery-time service builds a 90% prediction interval from two LightGBM models — objective='quantile' at alpha=0.05 and alpha=0.95. Monitoring flags that for a small share of inputs the interval is inverted: the 5th-percentile prediction exceeds the 95th. On-call suspects the serving layer swapped the outputs. Why can this happen with serving perfectly correct, and what is the honest handling?
choices: Nothing ties the two models together: each ensemble was trained independently to minimize its own pinball loss, and no constraint anywhere asserts q0.05(x) ≤ q0.95(x) for every x. Monotonicity across quantile levels is a property of the true distribution — separately-fit estimators do not inherit it, and in sparse or noisy regions of feature space the two fitted surfaces can cross. This is the known quantile-crossing artifact, not a bug. Handle it explicitly: sort or clip the predicted quantiles at serving time, or use a joint or monotonicity-constrained approach if ordering must hold by construction. The general lesson: an invariant that spans multiple independently trained models is yours to enforce — neither model's loss ever saw it

One model's alpha was silently left at the default — LightGBM's quantile objective defaults to 0.9, not 0.5 — so the 'lower' model is actually predicting a high quantile; auditing the training configs will surface the inversion

The placeholder hessian is the culprit: pinball loss has zero true curvature, so quantile leaf values wobble during training; more n_estimators and a lower learning_rate will converge the crossings away
Prediction intervals cannot be assembled from two point models — an interval needs a distributional model; the correct construction is a single mean regressor plus ±z·σ estimated from the residuals
questions.explanation: The reasoning error being tested is assuming that a property of the thing being estimated transfers to the estimators. True conditional quantiles are monotone in α by definition; but each trained model is just a function that made its own pinball loss small, and the α=0.05 model's errors owe nothing to the α=0.95 model's. Where data is dense, both surfaces track their targets and stay ordered; where it is sparse, each extrapolates its own way and they can cross — which is why the symptom is localized to a small share of inputs, the signature that distinguishes crossing from a systematic misconfiguration. The handling is a deliberate design decision: post-hoc monotone rearrangement (sorting the predicted quantiles) is cheap, standard, and provably does not worsen pinball loss, making it the pragmatic serving-time fix; joint or constrained estimation buys ordering by construction at the cost of a more complex training setup. The distractors reach for adjacent truths: the alpha=0.9 default is a real trap, but a mis-set α inverts or squeezes the interval systematically across the whole input space, not sporadically; the fake hessian genuinely makes quantile training more tuning-sensitive, yet no amount of convergence installs a cross-model constraint that neither objective contains; and mean ±z·σ is not the more correct construction — it assumes symmetric, homoscedastic errors, exactly the assumptions quantile-pair intervals exist to drop.
